question: Dividends 500cr, FCF 300cr. The 200cr gap is most likely funded by:
before: Dividends exceed FCF by 200cr -- must come from cash on BS or borrowing. A is wrong (dividends reduce RE). Revenue growth and depreciation are P&L/CFO concepts not direct dividend funding sources.
after:
Formula: Dividend Funding Gap = Dividends Paid − Free Cash Flow; where the gap must be financed from balance sheet sources (cash reserves) or income statement financing (new debt).

Step-by-step: Dividends paid are ₹500 cr. Free cash flow generated is ₹300 cr. The company has committed to paying out ₹500 cr but only generated ₹300 cr from operations and capital efficiency. The shortfall is ₹500 cr − ₹300 cr = ₹200 cr.

Result: A funding gap of ₹200 cr must be covered by either depleting existing cash balances on the balance sheet or raising new debt.

Why this is correct: Free cash flow represents cash available for all investors (debt holders and equity holders) after the company meets operating expenses and reinvestment needs. When dividends exceed FCF, the company cannot fund the payout from operational earnings alone and must tap external sources—either existing cash reserves or new borrowing.

Why the others are wrong: A) Increasing retained earnings is mechanically impossible because dividends by definition reduce retained earnings; paying out ₹500 cr decreases retained earnings, not increases it. C) Revenue growth is a forward-looking P&L driver and does not directly fund current dividend payments; growth takes time to convert to cash. D) Depreciation add-back is already embedded in FCF calculation (it is added back to net income to derive operating cash flow), so it does not represent an additional funding source for the dividend gap.

Intuition: Equity researchers must recognize that dividend sustainability depends on FCF, not accounting earnings. When dividends exceed FCF persistently, the company is either burning cash or increasing leverage—both red flags for dividend safety and credit quality. This is the core of dividend coverage analysis in equity research.
